extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing cozy/cosy mystery authors (genre fiction writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical conventions for writing cozy (cosy) mysteries: how to work within Golden Age-inspired genre constraints while adding originality, handling pacing, tone, setting, characterization, and reader expectations to produce satisfying, marketable cozy crime novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staying within genre constraints while adding variation
rubrics_metrics.description: A major challenge with formula writing is that of staying within genre constraints while adding enough variation to make the work unique and interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that cosy mysteries are formulaic and shaped by prior works (intertextuality); readers expect familiar elements but also 'new layers' within each novel. Aim to balance recognizable conventions with distinct elements so readers remain satisfied rather than feel deprived of novelty. The author cites Lethem, Eliot and Bloom to argue that complete originality is rare, so focus on inventive combinations and fresh details rather than rejecting the formula entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide escapist satisfaction (safe resolution and justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosy mysteries are escapist: the criminal is always found and justice is served, giving readers a sense of safety and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write to enable readers to 'escape' and feel safe — avoid bleak or unresolved endings. Emphasise restoration of order, protection from external threats, and moral closure consistent with Maslow’s idea of the need for safety. The puzzle should conclude with the perpetrator revealed and justice enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to Golden Age conventions / Knox 'Decalogue' influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosy mysteries evolved from the Golden Age of Crime and many writers still adhere to the Decalogue or ten commandments described by Knox (1929).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of classical mystery rules (fair play, clues, restricted viewpoint, logical detection) that shaped reader expectations. Authors may follow or deliberately bend these rules, but knowing them informs choices about clue placement, red herrings, and detective competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate pacing for the subgenre
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosy mysteries tend to be written at a meandering pace where the plot unfolds gradually in an enclosed space; suspense thrillers require more tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match pacing to tone: use a gentler, gradual unfolding for cosy tales to develop community and character; for grittier PI or thriller stories create firmer hooks, tighter pacing, and earlier tension. Consider phrasing, scene openings, and the placement of hooks—especially at the start of a series or when switching to a grittier subseries (example: the author's shift to Carlos Jacobi PI required new pacing and hooks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting: enclosed, often small-community locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosy mysteries commonly take place in an enclosed space (e.g., an English country village or on board a cruise ship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contained, recognisable settings that support intimacy, community dynamics, and a limited suspect pool. Settings should reinforce the cosy atmosphere and provide plausible social connections among characters (the author’s examples: English village, cruise ship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and content: avoid explicit gore, coarse language, and sexual explicitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all crime fiction needs to be gory; cosy crime can — and often should — be 'clean' crime without bad language or explicit sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create page-turning tension without sensationalist shock value. Maintain an ethical stance that eschews graphic detail and gratuitous profanity; this preserves the cosy's appeal to readers seeking safer, less graphic thrills and opens a viable market niche for 'clean crime.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation: create relatable, well-drawn characters and integrate quirks
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be relatable and distinctive; quirks (e.g., deliberate long-windedness) must be incorporated so readers understand them as deliberate traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show, don't tell: weave character traits into dialogue and behaviour so readers recognise purpose (example: a brother-in-law scientist who is long-winded and an 'anorak'). Make characters people readers might know in real life to build empathy and believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzle design: engage readers to solve the mystery alongside the sleuth
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosy mysteries provide intellectual excitement by letting readers exercise their brains to solve the puzzle, working alongside the sleuth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide fair clues and logical deductions so attentive readers can piece things together. Balance red herrings and solution evidence so the reveal feels earned; ensure clues are embedded in prose rather than gratuitously hidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening hooks and strong phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: When moving to grittier crime or simply wanting stronger engagement, consider phrasing and creating hooks at the beginning of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in compelling opening lines/scenes to draw readers in—especially important when changing subtone (e.g., from cosy to grittier PI fiction). Tight, engaging phrasing improves pace and reader retention across the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for genre value and market awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Formula literature (like crime fiction) has cultural value and fulfils a psychological function; there is room in the market for clean crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat genre work as valuable writing with a clear purpose: entertain, provide pleasure, and meet reader needs. Be aware of market niches (clean crime, cosy fans) and write to meet those expectations without feeling obliged to emulate shock-driven bestsellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage reader expectations through intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers and writers are influenced by previous books (intertextuality); readers expect to find familiar elements and new layers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge genre antecedents and use intertextual references or familiar motifs to satisfy readers while introducing twists or deeper layers. Failing to provide expected genre signposts can lead to reader dissatisfaction.
